page_metadata.title: Development of PBPK Models for PFOA and PFOS for Human Pregnancy and Lactation Life Stages
page_metadata.journal: Journal of toxicology and environmental health. Part A

model_classification.evidence_quote: Physiological parameters for PBPK models for PFOA and PFOS in pregnant woman and fetus.

model_context.model_origin: adapted from previously developed PBPK models for PFOA/PFOS for adult humans and rats during gestation and lactation and from existing human pregnancy and lactation models developed for other chemicals
model_context.stated_purpose: to understand how the physiological changes associated with development affect pharmacokinetics of PFOA and PFOS in the mother, fetus, and infant; to estimate maternal exposure from blood or milk concentrations; to examine integrative exposure and internal dose during in utero and postnatal periods; to predict internal dose in fetus or neonate resulting from maternal exposure
model_context.dose_metric: total plasma AUC in the mother and fetus (at embryonic week 39) for gestation models; total maternal plasma AUC and infant body AUC (at 6 months postpartum) for lactation models
model_context.original_application: PBPK models for PFOA/PFOS for adult humans and rats during gestation and lactation
model_context.current_application: PBPK models for PFOA and PFOS for gestation and lactation life stages in humans to estimate maternal exposure and predict internal dose in fetus and infant
model_context.source_quote: These models were derived from PBPK models for PFOA/PFOS that were previously developed for adult humans and rats during gestation and lactation and from existing human pregnancy and lactation models developed for other chemicals.

adme_determinant_evidence.description: Body weight scaling of tissue volumes in the mother
adme_determinant_evidence.evidence_quote: All of the tissue volumes in the mother are scaled to BW (and maternal BW increases by approximately 25 kg during pregnancy)

adme_determinant_evidence.description: Glomerular filtration rate (QFil) affects elimination rate
adme_determinant_evidence.evidence_quote: the flow to the filtrate compartment will affect how quickly the chemical is eliminated

adme_determinant_evidence.description: Free fraction of chemical in plasma controls tissue uptake and filtration
adme_determinant_evidence.evidence_quote: the free fraction of chemical controls how much chemical will be available for tissue uptake or filtration

adme_determinant_evidence.description: Fat volume constitutes a large percentage of body weight, increasing during pregnancy
adme_determinant_evidence.evidence_quote: Fat volume also constitutes a large % BW in humans (approximately 20% of BW in non-pregnant women), especially in pregnant women (approximately 30% of BW) as this increases as the pregnancy progresses.

adme_determinant_evidence.description: Placental transfer rate constants affect fetal plasma AUC
adme_determinant_evidence.evidence_quote: the bidirectional placental transfer rate constants (ktrans1c and ktrans2c)

adme_determinant_evidence.description: Maternal renal resorption parameters determine chemical availability for fetal transfer
adme_determinant_evidence.evidence_quote: The fetal plasma AUC is also affected by the maternal renal resorption parameters (Tm and Kt) as these will determine how much chemical is eliminated from the maternal system rather than being available for transfer to the fetus.

adme_determinant_evidence.description: Milk transfer rate constant determines chemical transfer from breast milk to nursing infant
adme_determinant_evidence.evidence_quote: KmilkC will determine how quickly the chemical is then transferred from breast milk to the nursing infant, and the infant AUC is more sensitive to this parameter than the mother's plasma AUC.

adme_phase_evidence.mathematical_implementation: Modeled as generic IV input to plasma compartment

adme_phase_evidence.mathematical_implementation: Tissue volumes as fractions of BW; amniotic fluid compartment with diffusion transfer rates

stated_assumptions.description: Amniotic fluid compartment included in both rat and human models based on rat data showing PFAAs present in amniotic fluid
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: Data in rats showed that PFAAs are present in amniotic fluid ; thus, an amniotic fluid compartment was included in the rat models and also in the human models presented here.

stated_assumptions.description: Transfer rates between amniotic fluid and fetal body described as simple diffusion
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: Transfer rates between the amniotic fluid compartment and the fetal body are described as simple diffusion (ktrans3C and ktrans4C; Table 3).

stated_assumptions.description: Volumes of liver, kidney, filtrate, and gut remained constant fractions of prepregnancy maternal body weight
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: Volumes of liver, kidney, filtrate, and gut remained constant fractions of the prepregnancy (non-pregnant) maternal body weight (BWinit); fractional volumes of these tissues for nonpregnant women was taken from .

stated_assumptions.description: Filtrate compartment set at 10% of kidney volume; model not sensitive to this value
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: The filtrate compartment, as in the adult human model, was set at 10% of the kidney volume (the model is not sensitive to this value).

stated_assumptions.description: Mammary tissue volume changes during lactation lumped with remaining maternal tissue volume
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: Because the volume of mammary tissue changes during lactation, these volume changes were accounted for by lumping this change in volume in with the remaining maternal tissue volume.

stated_assumptions.description: Renal plasma flow assumed to be approximately 5 times GFR due to lack of available data on renal plasma flow changes during lactation
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: Since there were no available data on renal plasma flow changes during lactation, renal plasma flow was assumed to be approximately 5 times that of the GFR (GFR is normally approximately 20% of renal plasma flow).

stated_assumptions.description: Maternal exposure modeled as generic IV input to plasma compartment because contributions from different exposure routes are not well understood
stated_assumptions.evidence_quote: maternal PFOA and PFOS exposure was modeled as a generic input to the plasma compartment (designated as "IV" in Figures 1 and 2) as contributions of PFAA exposure from different exposure routes are not well understood

stated_assumptions.description: Constant exposure assumed over a 24-hour time period for exposure estimation

All of the tissue volumes in the mother are scaled to BW (and maternal BW increases by approximately 25 kg during pregnancy)
the flow to the filtrate compartment will affect how quickly the chemical is eliminated
the free fraction of chemical controls how much chemical will be available for tissue uptake or filtration

Fat volume also constitutes a large % BW in humans (approximately 20% of BW in non-pregnant women), especially in pregnant women (approximately 30% of BW) as this increases as the pregnancy progresses.
the bidirectional placental transfer rate constants (ktrans1c and ktrans2c)

The fetal plasma AUC is also affected by the maternal renal resorption parameters (Tm and Kt) as these will determine how much chemical is eliminated from the maternal system rather than being available for transfer to the fetus.
KmilkC will determine how quickly the chemical is then transferred from breast milk to the nursing infant, and the infant AUC is more sensitive to this parameter than the mother's plasma AUC.
Data in rats showed that PFAAs are present in amniotic fluid ; thus, an amniotic fluid compartment was included in the rat models and also in the human models presented here.
Transfer rates between the amniotic fluid compartment and the fetal body are described as simple diffusion (ktrans3C and ktrans4C; Table 3).

Volumes of liver, kidney, filtrate, and gut remained constant fractions of the prepregnancy (non-pregnant) maternal body weight (BWinit); fractional volumes of these tissues for nonpregnant women was taken from .
The filtrate compartment, as in the adult human model, was set at 10% of the kidney volume (the model is not sensitive to this value).
